## (Computer Exercise) Let us practice unit root tests on the following series. (All series have been seasonally adjusted.).

```{r message = FALSE}
library("quantmod")
library(forecast)
library(tseries)
library(urca)
library(ggplot2)
```


## (a) Series #1: Logarithm of US quarterly real GDP from 1947Q1 to 2019Q4. 
```{r}
getSymbols("GDP", src = "FRED")
lgdp<-log(GDP)['/2019']
```
## i. Examine the time series plot and ACF of lgdp.
```{r}
plot(lgdp)
```
```{r}
Acf(lgdp)
```

The time series and autocorrelation plot is showing non-stationary view. Specially Autocorrelation is showing high serially correlated time series that decays very slowly. 

## ii. Perform the augmented Dickey-Fuller test of the null hypothesis that lgdp is difference stationary against the alternative that it is trend stationary.

```{r}
result <- ur.df(lgdp, type="trend",lag=6, selectlags = "AIC")
summary(result) 
```
```{r}
plot(result)
```
According the augmented Dickey-Fuller test result, we fail to reject the null hypothesis in favor of alternative hypothesis at the 5% significance level, which said the time series is not stationary or it is likely difference stationary.


## Series #2: Growth rate of US quarterly real GDP from 1947Q2 to 2019Q4. Use the data in part (a) to generate the GDP growth series as follows:
```{r}
gdpgr <-100 * diff(lgdp)[-1]
```
## i. Examine the time series plot and ACF of gdpgr.
```{r}
plot(gdpgr)
```
```{r}
acf(gdpgr)
```
Visually the difference times series looks stationary. Also, autocorrelation is showing that it is decreasing 

## ii. Perform the augmented Dickey-Fuller test of the null hypothesis of a unit root.

```{r}
result <- ur.df(gdpgr, type="drift",  selectlags="AIC")
summary(result) 
```
```{r}
plot(result)
```

According the augmented Dickey-Fuller test result we can reject the null hypothesis in favor of alternative hypothesis at the 5% significance level which said the series is stationary.

## iii. Based on your test results for lgdp and gdpgr, do you think it is appropriate to apply stationary ARMA models to the difference of log of real GDP?

According the those test we can say that diff(lgdp) which is the difference of log of GDP is stationary and we can apply ARMA to model it. 

## (c) Series #3: US quarterly inflation rate from 1960Q2 to 2019Q4. First retrieve the quarterly Consumer Price Index (CPI) series from FRED and then compute the inflation rate as the difference of logs.

```{r}
cpi <- getSymbols("CPALTT01USQ661S", src = "FRED", auto.assign = FALSE)
inf <- 100 * diff(log(cpi))[-1]
```
## i. Examine the time series plot and ACF of inf.

```{r}
plot(inf)
```

```{r}
acf(inf)
```

Visually we can say that the inf time series is not stationary. Also, Autocorrelation is showing highly serially correlated lags that decays slowly. 

## ii. Perform the augmented Dickey-Fuller and KPSS tests to investigate whether inf is stationary.
```{r}
result <- ur.df(inf, type="drift",lags = 6,selectlags = "AIC")
summary(result) 
```

```{r}
plot(result)
```
From ADF test, we can reject null hypothesis, so the times series is likely stationary, which is in contrast with our visual observation.

```{r}
kpss.test(inf, "Level")
```


```{r}
result <- ur.kpss(inf, type="mu", lags="short")
summary(result)
```
From KPSS test, we can reject null hypothesis which said that time series is not stationary. 
From these two tests, we can see ADF and KPSS are in contrast from each other, so we should conider more evidence.

## iii. Perform the augmented Dickey-Fuller and KPSS tests to investigate whether the first difference of inf is stationary.


```{r}
dinf<-diff(inf)[-1]
```

```{r}
plot(dinf)
```
```{r}
acf(dinf)
```
Visually we can say that difference of inflation is stationary

```{r}
result<-ur.df(dinf,type="none")
summary(result)
```
```{r}
plot(result)
```
From ADF test, we can reject null hypothesis which said that our series likely is stationary

```{r}
result <-ur.kpss(dinf, , type="mu", lags="short")
summary(result)
```
From KPSS test we fail to reject the null hypothesis, so the series is stationary. 
## iv. In practice, many forecasters treat US inflation as I(1). Are your findings consistent with this view?
Since both ADF and KPSS test are aligned in the results, we can say more strongly that inflation can be considdred as I(1).
